content: A fluid-resistant medical or surgical mask with a structured design, such as a duckbill or cup shape, is recommended to prevent the mask from collapsing against the mouth. Additionally, either a face shield or goggles should be worn for eye protection. When removing personal protective equipment (PPE), it is crucial to avoid contact between soiled items, such as gloves or gowns, and the face (eyes, nose, or mouth). Clinical and non-clinical personnel should be assigned exclusively to viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF) patient care areas and should not move freely between isolation areas and other clinical zones during an outbreak. The use of needles and other sharp objects should be minimized, and precautions should be taken when preparing medications for injection or inserting IVs. Phlebotomy and laboratory testing should be limited to essential diagnostic evaluations and patient care. PPE should be worn by all healthcare workers providing direct care to suspected VHF patients, support staff cleaning isolation rooms or handling contaminated supplies, laboratory staff processing patient specimens, burial teams handling deceased VHF patients, family members caring for VHF patients, and anyone entering high-risk zones. Hand hygiene is essential at all times. Facilities should provide clean running water, soap, single-use towels, and alcohol-based hand rubs. Alcohol-based hand rubs are the standard of care and should be available at every point of care. Hands should be washed with soap and water when visibly dirty and disinfected with alcohol-based hand rubs when they appear clean. Artificial nails or nail extensions should not be worn, and jewelry such as rings, watches, or bracelets should be avoided. Hands should be dried with single-use towels before starting any activity. Gloves should be disinfected within high-risk zones as needed and changed between patients. When caring for multiple patients in the same room, complete care for one patient before moving to the next. Gloves should be changed using a two-step process: disinfect the outer gloves before removing them, then disinfect the inner gloves before donning a clean outer pair. Respiratory hygiene should be practiced by all staff, patients, and visitors. This includes covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, using tissues or the inner surface of the arm, and performing hand hygiene after contact with respiratory secretions. Tissues should be disposed of in no-touch receptacles. Patients with respiratory symptoms should maintain spatial separation of at least one meter from others and use tissues or masks to cover their nose and mouth. To prevent injuries from needles and sharp instruments, handle them with care, avoid bending or recapping used needles, and dispose of them immediately in puncture-resistant containers. Cleaning and disinfection of the environment should follow strict protocols, with cleaning performed from clean to dirty areas to prevent contamination. Reusable equipment should be cleaned, disinfected, and sterilized appropriately before use with another patient. Disposable items should be discarded immediately after use in leak-proof, clearly labeled bags. Contaminated linens should be handled with full PPE and disinfected or incinerated if heavily soiled. PPE should be donned under supervision, starting with hand hygiene, gloves, coveralls, masks, face shields or goggles, and aprons. Doffing should also be supervised, with careful removal of each item to avoid self-contamination. Hand hygiene should be performed at every step of the process. Spraying disinfectants in clinical areas is discouraged as it has no proven disease control benefit and may aerosolize pathogens. However, spraying may be acceptable in specific outdoor or community settings, such as decontaminating households of Ebola victims. Proper use of PPE, hand hygiene, and environmental cleaning are critical to infection prevention and control during VHF outbreaks.
